bp: Many data-hungry systems now face an awkward bargain. Real text written by people is costly to gather, can expose private facts, and may be locked inside product or research pipelines. Synthetic text offers a tempting substitute: ask a generative model to produce reviews, comments, or paper-review-like examples, then train another model on that cheaper collection. The danger is that the generator tends to repeat the common middle of the source collection. Unusual styles, difficult cases, rare opinions, and high-uncertainty examples can fade out. This paper studies that failure as model collapse: repeated reuse of generated outputs contracts the learned distribution, meaning the generated collection covers a narrower slice of the original world. DASGen is built for the practical job of making synthetic text that still covers rare tail regions, not just fluent common cases, so downstream training data remains broad enough for long-tailed applications.
wh: The hard part is that rare text is rare for a reason: there are few examples, and a generator has learned that common patterns are safer. If a Yelp-like review collection mostly contains ordinary restaurant comments, a model can generate many plausible ordinary reviews while barely touching unusual phrasing, edge-case sentiment, uncommon topics, or difficult reviewer behavior. That looks acceptable if one only checks fluency or average quality. It fails when the synthetic data becomes training material, because the next model sees a world with the uncommon parts weakened or missing. The abstract gives a concrete sign: when models are iteratively trained on their own synthetic outputs, the upper tail of the perplexity distribution compresses, with high-percentile values dropping by nearly half. Perplexity here is a measure of how unsurprising text looks to a model. If the most surprising examples become much less surprising, diversity has been squeezed out.
naive: A smart beginner would generate a large synthetic corpus with a strong hosted language model, perhaps using broad prompts such as "write more Yelp reviews" or "write more ICLR reviews," then mix those outputs into training. If the generated text is grammatical and resembles the domain, the beginner might assume more data means better coverage. The failure is that volume does not guarantee variety. A generator can produce thousands of examples while circling the same common region of the data. Another beginner fix is random prompting, but randomness still follows the model's learned habit of choosing likely continuations. Without a deliberate way to find and refill underrepresented regions, synthetic data can make the training set cleaner-looking while quietly erasing rare features.
ap: DASGen's central move is to treat synthetic generation as a coverage problem before treating it as a writing problem. First it looks for parts of the existing data distribution that are underrepresented. The abstract says it does this through embedding-space mining: it turns texts into learned numeric descriptions of meaning and style, then searches that map for regions that need more examples. That term matters only after translation: the method is building a map where nearby texts are treated as similar, then asking which neighborhoods are thin. Second, it steers a frozen, hosted language model with semantically structured prompts, so the generator is directed toward those thin neighborhoods. Third, it uses a discriminative diversity objective, a scoring rule that rewards outputs that add distinguishable variety rather than merely sounding normal. The base model is not retrained; the intervention is in selection, prompting, and diversity-guided generation.
mech: The input is an existing text collection from a domain such as Yelp reviews or ICLR'25 reviews, plus access to a hosted large language model that can generate new text. DASGen first represents each real example as a point in a comparison map, where distance is meant to capture semantic similarity. Because the abstract calls the method tail-aware, the next step is to search this map for tail regions: neighborhoods that exist in the source distribution but have weak coverage or are at risk of being lost when ordinary generation overproduces common cases. Those regions become generation targets. Instead of asking the language model for generic new reviews, DASGen builds semantically structured prompts that describe the kind of content needed from a target region. The language model remains frozen, meaning its internal weights are not updated; DASGen controls it from the outside. Candidate generated texts are then judged by a discriminative diversity objective. In plain terms, the system compares candidates against the desired rare region and against one another, preferring examples that enrich the tail rather than duplicate already common text. The output is a synthetic corpus intended to be distribution-aligned: it should resemble the source collection while deliberately restoring coverage of rare regions. The evaluations then check tail coverage and downstream accuracy on Yelp and ICLR'25 review settings.
math: The first mathematical idea is distribution matching. A distribution is the shape of a collection: which kinds of examples are common, which are rare, and how far the rare cases stretch from the center. DASGen is not only asking whether each generated text is plausible; it is asking whether the whole generated pile has a similar shape to the original pile, especially in the tail. The second idea is similarity geometry. Texts are compressed into numeric descriptions so the system can measure which examples are near one another. This compression is useful because it turns vague semantic coverage into a searchable map, but it can lose details if the map preserves the wrong kind of likeness. The third idea is tail measurement. The abstract uses the upper tail of the perplexity distribution as evidence of diversity loss: highly surprising texts should remain present if the collection still contains difficult or unusual cases. The fourth idea is objective-guided selection. A discriminative diversity objective defines what counts as better synthetic text, not as a human aesthetic judgment but as a score that favors distinct, tail-enriching candidates. The central tradeoff is coverage versus fidelity: generated examples must move into rare regions without drifting into text that no longer belongs to the domain.
dots: This paper connects to the conference's language-model and text-mining work because it asks whether generated language preserves the evidence structure of the collection it came from. It sits near similarity papers because its first step depends on a map of texts where distance stands in for semantic relatedness, and the success of tail mining depends on that map being faithful. It also connects to probability and information ideas: the tail is about unlikely or surprising cases, and the paper treats the disappearance of high-perplexity examples as an information loss, not just a cosmetic change in writing style. Compared with retrieval and recommendation papers that choose useful items from a large pile, DASGen chooses useful generation targets from a source distribution. Compared with privacy-motivated synthetic-data work, it accepts the privacy and curation appeal of synthetic content but argues that usefulness depends on preserving rare features that generic generation tends to smooth away.
ww: The approach should work better than naive generation because it interrupts the self-reinforcing preference for common cases. A general language model is good at producing fluent examples that fit the center of a domain, because those are the patterns it can satisfy with high confidence. DASGen first asks where the center is not enough. By mining the semantic map, it turns an invisible absence into explicit targets: these are the regions where more examples are needed. Structured prompts then give the frozen model a narrower assignment than open-ended generation, so it is more likely to produce text with the intended rare properties. The diversity objective adds a second guardrail. If two generated candidates say the same kind of thing in slightly different wording, they do not add much coverage; if a candidate occupies a thin but relevant region, it is more valuable. This matches the mechanism to the failure mode. Model collapse is a shrinking of variety, so DASGen spends its effort widening the generated collection where shrinkage is most damaging.
po: The payoff is a training-free way to make synthetic text corpora that better preserve long-tail coverage. The abstract reports strong tail coverage on two review settings: 98.54% on Yelp and 92.00% on ICLR'25, along with improved downstream accuracy compared with competitive baselines. The practical capability is not merely producing more text. It is producing synthetic data that remains useful when rare features matter, while still fitting into existing data pipelines because the hosted language model is frozen and no retraining of that generator is required. For teams using synthetic data to reduce curation cost or privacy exposure, DASGen gives a concrete method for checking and repairing a major failure mode.
limits: The claims depend on the text map capturing the rare features that matter. If the learned numeric descriptions group examples by surface wording while missing the real tail property, DASGen may enrich the wrong regions. The method also assumes that semantically structured prompts can make a frozen hosted model produce valid rare-region examples rather than strained or unrealistic text. The abstract reports Yelp and ICLR'25 review evaluations, so broader domains are not proven here. It gives tail coverage and downstream accuracy, but does not establish privacy guarantees, human quality judgments, behavior under adversarial prompts, or whether generated tail examples preserve every factual and cultural detail present in real rare cases.
